catalog_quote: Delafosse (1900:15-18) remarked more than one hundred twenty years ago that Anyi was not a full-fledged tone language like Yoruba, nor was it an accent language like English or French. ... I concur with them that Anyi is hard to classify suprasegmentally because it straddles the three prosodic types into which world languages are currently classified, namely: tone languages, pitch-accent languages, and accent languages. ... After nearly 40 years of continuous research on Anyi, I have found only about 60 lexical minimal pairs and 14 triplets (see Appendix). The data comes from a corpus of 4,539 words. In other words, the RFL of pitch-based minimal pairs and triplets is 1.63% ... To be clear, I’m not claiming that Anyi is not a tonal language. All I’m saying is that it does fit traditional prosodic taxonomies. Therefore, its tonal status is unsettled because it straddles all existing typo…
sweep_summary: Two title-hit items for Anyi (anyi1245, catalog = tonal, deciding source Koffi 2022). (1) Gut/Urua/Adouakou/Gibbon 2002 (TAPS proceedings) was found open on Dafydd Gibbon's Bielefeld author page in two versions (print and web edition), both saved and read in full: it is a speech-rhythm study (RI/RR/%V-deltaC) that classifies Anyi as syllable-timed and describes it as a tone language with H, L, LH, HL (mid from sandhi); it never mentions word stress or accent for Anyi, so it confirms the tonal coding only indirectly and does not supersede Koffi 2022. Note the Glottolog byline order (Gibbon first) differs from the PDF (Gut, Urua, Adouakou & Gibbon). (2) Leben & Ahoua 1997 'Prosodic domains in Baule' (Phonology 14(1):113-132, correct DOI 10.1017/S0952675797003321) is about Baule, the sister Bia language, not Anyi; only the abstract is reachable (Cambridge paywall; landing page saved); it discusses L/H tone, downdrift and prosodic-word domains, nothing on stress; silent on Anyi, low priority for this record (would matter for baou1238). Bonus open items pulled from the same author page and the TAPS TOC and Gibbon, Ahoua & Adjepole 2011 (ICPhS XVII, Anyi awosi dirges; underlying H/L with spreading and downstep, minimal pairs, no stress), Ahoua, Adjepole & Gibbon 2009 (1-page abstract, tone-tune in Anyi Sanvi songs), Gibbon 2002 TAPS keynote (p.16 lists 'freely combinable tones on nouns, restricted tones on verbs (Anyi-Baule)', which matches Koffi 2022's predictable-verb-tone point), and Anyanwu 2001 'On the manifestation of stress in African languages' and Leben 2001 'Tonal feet' (both TAPS; neither mentions Anyi or Baule). Nothing read contradicts or refines the catalog's 'tonal' classification; no source states a word-stress position for Anyi. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs could not be reached by automated download.

new_statements.quote: Phonetic long vowels occur but their analysis as a sequence of two vowels has been suggested, which is corroborated by the fact that they almost always have a complex tone. Words with contrasting vowel length therefore always also have a tonal contrast. ... Anyi has four phonological tones: Two level tones, H and L, and two contour tones, rising LH and falling HL. The appearance of a mid tone is due to the effect of tone sandhi rules.
new_statements.citation: Gut, Ulrike, Eno-Abasi Urua, Sandrine Adouakou & Dafydd Gibbon. 2002. Rhythm in West African tone languages: a study of Ibibio, Anyi and Ega. In U. Gut & D. Gibbon (eds.), Typology of African Prosodic Systems (Bielefeld Occasional Papers in Typology 1), 159-165.
new_statements.locator: p. 161, sec. 3.1 'Anyi' (print pagination; same passage on p. 3 of the web-edition PDF)
new_statements.reading: A first-hand instrumental study (co-authored by an Anyi-speaking linguist, Sandrine Adouakou) that treats Anyi as a tone language with two level tones H/L and two contours LH/HL (mid tone = sandhi), measures its rhythm as syllable-timed, and describes no word stress or accent position at all. This is consistent with the catalog's 'tonal' coding but it is a rhythm paper, not a stress/accent statement; it adds nothing on the Koffi 2022 'straddles typologies' question. A second open first-hand statement downloaded as a bonus (Gibbon, Ahoua & Adjepole 2011, ICPhS XVII, sec. 2.3, file) says: 'There are two lexicalised contrastive tones, H and L.. with complex realisations due to spreading as HL, LH.. downstep.. yielding a terraced pitch downtrend', with lexical tonal minimal pairs, again with no mention of stress.

new_statements.quote: Le ton est aux langues à tons, ce qu'est l'accent aux langues telles que le français, l'anglais, l'allemand etc. Cependant, cette définition reste ambiguë, car on pourrait poser la question de savoir ce qu'on entend par accent. L'accent consiste en la mise en valeur d'une syllabe dans chaque mot en isolation. En français par exemple, l'accent tombe sur la dernière syllabe du mot. Le ton quant à lui, est la hauteur mélodique perçue sur chaque syllabe d'un mot donné. [p. 5] ... Ainsi donc on retient en grande partie que les tons sont aux langues à tons ce que les accents sont aux langues telles le français, l'anglais, l'allemand etc. [p. 190]
new_statements.translation: Tone is to tone languages what accent is to languages such as French, English, German etc. However, this definition remains ambiguous, since one could ask what is meant by accent. Accent consists in the highlighting of one syllable in each word in isolation. In French, for example, the accent falls on the last syllable of the word. Tone, on the other hand, is the melodic pitch perceived on each syllable of a given word. [p. 5] ... Thus we retain, in large part, that tones are to tone languages what accents are to languages such as French, English, German etc. [p. 190]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's tonal coding and with the existing Gut/Urua/Adouakou/Gibbon 2002 statement (four tones H, L, LH, HL, mid = sandhi, no word stress). Same author, same variety (Indénié).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Same document as index 3 (the hdl.handle.net link resolves to pure.mpg.de/pubman/item/item_407552, which could not be reached by automated download with an Anubis challenge; the thesis itself was read from the DNB long-term-archive copy). Anyi (Indénié variety) is treated throughout as a tone language with four phonological tones (H, L, LH, HL; a mid tone exists only phonetically, from tone-sandhi). The thesis never assigns a word-level accent/stress position; 'accent' in the sense of one prominent syllable per word is explicitly the property of French/English/German, contrasted with the tone Anyi has. The only 'accent' the thesis recognizes in Anyi is the phrase-level focus pitch accent (sec. 5.6.2.1). The phonetic-correlate chapter (3.2.3) measures duration and F0 as correlates of tone, not of stress; intensity is treated only as an intonational/emotive parameter (6.2.3).
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: contour tones (LH, HL) in di-/polysyllables sit on a single syllable, 'très souvent' the final one (p. 59).
new_statements.identity_note: Adouakou 2005/2006 describes the Indénié (Ndénié) variety of Anyi spoken around Abengourou, eastern Côte d'Ivoire; the thesis cites Retord 1972 (Sanvi), Jaboulay 1974 (Indénié) and Quaireau 1978 (Morofoué/general) as all finding the same four tones. Quaireau 1987 (unopened) covers the Moronou, Ndénié and Bona varieties; Keïta 2008 (unopened) treats 'agni' generally. All fall under Glottolog anyi1245.

new_statements.quote: L'agni qui est une langue à ton, admet 4 tons phonologiquement pertinents. [p. 98] ... L'accent de focalisation est ce qu'en anglais, on appelle Pitch accent. Bien que l'agni soit une langue à ton, la manifestation de cet accent de focalisation est observée dans sa structure intonative. Etant donné que le mot marqué possède déjà un ton, la perception de l'accent de focalisation est possible grâce à l'allongement du ton déjà existant de la syllabe où il opère. [p. 144] ... En résumé, nous retenons que le ton moyen en agni a plutôt un statut phonétique. [p. 58]
new_statements.translation: Anyi, which is a tone language, admits 4 phonologically relevant tones. [p. 98] ... The focus accent is what in English is called Pitch accent. Although Anyi is a tone language, the manifestation of this focus accent is observed in its intonational structure. Since the marked word already has a tone, the perception of the focus accent is made possible by the lengthening of the already-existing tone of the syllable on which it operates. [p. 144] ... In sum, we hold that the mid tone in Anyi has rather a phonetic status. [p. 58]

new_statements.rule_in_words: The bieson.ub.uni-bielefeld.de PDF URL (and pub.uni-bielefeld.de) now sit behind an Anubis challenge; the Internet Archive has only the 2007 BieSOn record page, not the PDF. Reading: Anyi Indénié is a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and two contour tones (LH, HL) on lexical items, a phonetic mid tone from sandhi, downdrift/downstep rules; no word stress or fixed accent position is described anywhere; the only 'accent' is a phrase-level focus pitch accent realised by lengthening the tone-bearing syllable, with marked syllables observed at phrase end before a pause. Tone chapter TOC: 3.2.2 Système tonal, 3.2.2.1 Inventaire des tons lexicaux, 3.2.2.2 Paires minimales, 3.2.2.3 Règles tonales, 3.2.3 Corrélats phonétiques du ton (durée, F0).

tone_statements.citation: Koffi, Ettien N. 2018. Acoustic phonetic measurements of grammatical tones in Anyi. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 143(3_Supplement): 1967 (meeting abstract). DOI 10.1121/1.5036474
tone_statements.quote: Talkers and hearers of Anyi, a West African language of the Akan family, are very adept at discriminating between sentences containing verbs conjugated in the indicative, the intentional, and the subjunctive moods just by relying on subtle variations in pitch. ... The tone bearing units (TBU) on the subject pronoun and the disyllabic verbs are analyzed acoustically. ... The F0 of the subject pronoun and of the verb are the most robust cues for discriminating between the declarative and the intentional moods. The differentiation between the intentional and the subjunctive moods rests principally on the F0 of the subject pronoun.
tone_statements.summary: Grammatical mood tones on pronoun and verb; F0 primary cue.

tone_statements.quote: There are two lexicalised contrastive tones, H and L (marked with acute and grave diacritics), with complex realisations due to spreading as HL, LH (cf. Figure 4) downstep; cf. Connell [5]. Same-tone sequences remain nearly level and automatic downstep occurs, (the H-L fall in pitch is greater than the L-H rise, yielding a ‘terraced’ pitch downtrend). ... (note the rule which spreads H on to a following L yielding surface HL)
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.3 'Sound system', p. 2, plus the parenthesis from sec. 3.1 same page
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H L; H-spreading gives surface HL/LH; automatic downstep (terracing).

tone_statements.citation: Ahoua, Firmin, Kouamé Adjépolé & Dafydd Gibbon. 2009. Prosodic domains and tones in speech and songs in Anyi Sanvi. Abstract, 6th World Congress of African Linguistics (WOCAL 6), Cologne, August 2009. 1 p. PDF:https://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/gibbon/Dafydd_Gibbon_Publication_PDFs/2009_Ahoua_Adjepole_Gibbon_Prosodic_domains_and_tones_in_speech_and_songs_in_Anyi_Sanvi-03.pdf
tone_statements.quote: We focus on tone-melody relations in three songs in Anyi Sanvi. We use both a musical transcription and a narrow acoustic-phonetic analysis, and compare our results with lexical and the surface tones, noting on syllable structure. Our results suggest that tunes in these Anyi songs are ‘natural’ in the sense that they correspond well to tones in speech
tone_statements.summary: Lexical vs surface tones; song melody follows speech tones.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding Koffi 2022 quotation and the Delafosse 1900:115-116 secondary quotes are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated pages. (2) Deciding source is a 2022 phonology/typology article by a native-speaker phonetician; it is recent and on-topic but short and in an in-house journal, and it hedges ('straddles' typologies) while affirming Anyi is tonal. The larger descriptions (Quaireau 1987 675 pp, Keïta 2008 340 pp, Retord 1972) are not open. (3) Two open works downloaded now — Ahua 2004 (Osnabrück diss., pp.60-64) and Quaireau 1982 (Verbum, pp.178-179) — both describe Anyi as a two-register (H/L + contour) tone language with lexical tonal minimal pairs and tone sandhi, and neither describes word stress (Ahua's only 'accentuation' is phrase-level exclamative emphasis); Ahua also records the 'unanimité' of Retord 1972, Quaireau 1981 and Burmeister 1983

sources.citation: Gut, Ulrike, Eno-Abasi Urua, Sandrine Adouakou & Dafydd Gibbon. 2002. Rhythm in West African tone languages: a study of Ibibio, Anyi and Ega. In Ulrike Gut & Dafydd Gibbon (eds.), Typology of African Prosodic Systems (Bielefeld Occasional Papers in Typology 1), 159-165. [Glottolog id 47904 lists the byline as Gibbon, Gut, Adouakou & Urua; the PDF byline is Gut, Urua, Adouakou & Gibbon]
sources.quote: Anyi has four phonological tones: Two level tones, H and L, and two contour tones, rising LH and falling HL. The appearance of a mid tone is due to the effect of tone sandhi rules. [p.161] ... The aim of this paper is to describe three West African tone languages – Anyi, Ega and Ibibio – which have not been previously classified in terms of their speech rhythm. [p.159] ... All three languages exhibit a clear tendency towards syllable-timing, i.e. the difference in duration between adjacent syllables is relatively small. [p.163]
sources.locator: pp. 160-161, sec. 3.1 'Anyi'; results p. 163 Table 1; discussion p. 164
sources.note: Acoustic speech-rhythm study (one male Anyi speaker, 12 sentences of a 1.42-min narrative; Rhythm Index, Rhythm Ratio, Ramus %V/deltaC). Anyi is treated throughout as a 'West African tone language' with H, L, LH, HL (mid = sandhi) and is measured as syllable-timed (RR 65.8, RI 43.9). No word stress or accent position is described for Anyi anywhere in the paper; the only stress talk is the general Dauer (1983) discussion that syllable-timed languages 'either do not have lexical stress or accent is realized by variations in pitch contour' (p.160), which is not applied to Anyi specifically.

tone.quote: Talkers and hearers of Anyi, a West African language of the Akan family, are very adept at discriminating between sentences containing verbs conjugated in the indicative, the intentional, and the subjunctive moods just by relying on subtle variations in pitch. ... The tone bearing units (TBU) on the subject pronoun and the disyllabic verbs are analyzed acoustically. ... The F0 of the subject pronoun and of the verb are the most robust cues for discriminating between the declarative and the intentional moods. The differentiation between the intentional and the subjunctive moods rests principally on the F0 of the subject pronoun.

sources.quote: We focus on tone-melody relations in three songs in Anyi Sanvi. We use both a musical transcription and a narrow acoustic-phonetic analysis, and compare our results with lexical and the surface tones, noting on syllable structure. Our results suggest that tunes in these Anyi songs are ‘natural’ in the sense that they correspond well to tones in speech
